Newborn Care

When your baby is not gaining weight as expected

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Slow weight gain is a reason to look closely at feeding and health, not to compare your baby with a picture or blame yourself. The trend matters, and a baby who is sleepy, dehydrated or feeding poorly needs help promptly. A clear assessment can identify what support and nutrition are needed.

Look at your baby’s pattern, not an advertising picture

A healthy baby does not have to look like the round-cheeked baby on a nappy packet. Birth size, gestational age and family characteristics all influence appearance. The important questions are whether your baby is feeding effectively, staying hydrated and following an appropriate growth pattern over time.

If weight gain is slower than expected, arrange a feeding and medical review. That is a request for support, not an admission that you have done something wrong. Some babies need help transferring milk, some need a different feeding plan, and others need investigation for a health problem. A single photograph or comparison with another baby cannot make that distinction.

Early weight loss and return to birth weight

Some loss of weight in the first days after birth reflects normal fluid changes. The percentage must be interpreted alongside the baby’s age in hours, feeding, delivery circumstances and clinical condition. A loss of more than 10% of birth weight needs further evaluation; smaller losses can also need attention when feeding or hydration is concerning.

Many newborns regain birth weight in about 7–14 days. NICE notes that most have done so by three weeks, but that is not an instruction to wait three weeks with a poorly feeding baby. If weight is not recovering as expected, get advice and a repeat measurement. Tripling birth weight by around the first birthday is a broad average, not an individual deadline or a reason to overlook a faltering pattern.

Three broad reasons weight gain can slow

A baby needs enough usable energy for everyday functions and growth. Weight gain may slow because too little milk or food is reaching the baby, nutrients are being lost or poorly absorbed, or an illness increases energy needs. More than one factor can be present at the same time.

These categories guide assessment rather than provide a home diagnosis. The clinician may observe a feed, examine the baby and review growth and symptoms before deciding whether tests are needed. Many feeding problems become clearer through that observation; an otherwise well baby does not automatically need an extensive panel of blood tests.

1. Milk intake may be less than it appears

Frequent time at the breast does not always mean effective milk transfer, and finishing a particular bottle size does not establish that the daily intake is adequate. Newborns need frequent feeds, including overnight, but the appropriate frequency and amount depend on age, weight, feeding method and the reason for concern.

Avoid using one fixed formula volume or an exact three-hour schedule for every newborn. Review feeding cues, the number of feeds, bottle preparation and what happens during a feed with the care team. If the baby is not gaining, ask for a written plan that explains when to offer feeds, whether to wake the baby and how soon weight should be checked again.

Sleepiness and feeding coordination need attention

A mildly sleepy baby may become ready to feed with skin-to-skin contact, a nappy change or gentle repositioning. Keep the baby comfortably warm. Do not shake, repeatedly startle or chill a baby to make them feed. A baby who is unusually difficult to wake or cannot stay alert enough to feed needs urgent assessment, not repeated attempts at stimulation.

Sucking, swallowing and breathing need to work together. Some babies, especially those born early, tire quickly or have difficulty coordinating these skills. Coughing, choking, colour changes, sweating or marked breathlessness during feeds should be reported promptly. A feeding specialist can assess the mechanics and help make feeding both safer and more effective.

Attachment and milk transfer can often be improved

A breastfeeding assessment can look at positioning, attachment, swallowing, nipple pain and how the breast feels before and after a feed. Engorgement may make attachment harder, and support with softening the breast or positioning can help. Visible sucking alone is not enough to show that milk is being swallowed.

The baby’s mouth and tongue movement may also need assessment if feeding remains difficult. A suspected tongue-tie or lip-tie is not automatically the explanation, and appearance alone does not establish a need for a procedure. Ask a qualified clinician or lactation professional to assess function and the whole feed before selecting treatment.

Introducing solids should not abruptly displace milk

Complementary foods are generally introduced around six months when the baby is developmentally ready. Breast milk or infant formula remains an important source of nutrition through the first year. Early solids or large amounts of low-energy food can sometimes displace milk before the baby is getting enough nutrition from other foods.

If growth slows after starting solids, review both milk feeds and the types, amounts and textures of food offered. The answer is not automatically to stop all solids or force larger meals. A clinician or paediatric dietitian can suggest age-appropriate, nutrient-rich foods while preserving a suitable milk intake.

2. Vomiting and absorption problems are different

Ordinary small spit-ups are common and often occur in babies who grow well. More significant vomiting or painful feeding can reduce how much nutrition stays in the body. Reflux is not itself the same as failure to absorb nutrients, and slow growth should not automatically be labelled reflux without assessment.

Persistent forceful vomiting, green or yellow-green vomit, blood in vomit, a swollen painful abdomen or a baby who seems unwell needs urgent medical attention. Report chronic diarrhoea, blood in stools or marked feeding distress too. Do not add thickeners, cereal or acid-suppressing medicine as a weight-gain remedy without a specific clinical plan.

Food allergy and coeliac disease need proper diagnosis

Cow’s-milk protein allergy can sometimes contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms and poor growth. It is different from lactose intolerance. Broadly removing foods from a breastfeeding parent’s diet or repeatedly switching formula without guidance can make nutrition harder to manage and can obscure the diagnosis.

Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated response to gluten that can damage the intestine and impair absorption after gluten is introduced. It is not simply difficulty digesting dairy or a usual immediate food allergy. If it is suspected, discuss testing before starting a gluten-free diet because removing gluten can affect test results. Any necessary exclusion diet should include a plan to replace the missing nutrients.

Jaundice can be linked with feeding difficulty

Jaundice means yellowing caused by bilirubin and is common in newborns. Poor intake, dehydration and jaundice can occur together, and a jaundiced baby may be sleepy and feed less effectively. This is not a simple digestive absorption problem and should be assessed in the context of the baby’s age and condition.

Tell the maternity or paediatric team if jaundice is worsening, feeding is poor or the baby is unusually sleepy. Changes in urine or stool also matter. The team may measure bilirubin and assess feeding and hydration. Do not rely on sunlight, water or repeated attempts to feed an unresponsive baby instead of seeking care.

3. Prematurity, breathing and heart conditions can increase needs

Babies born before 37 weeks may have different nutritional needs and less stamina or coordination for feeding. Follow-up uses appropriate growth assessment, including corrected age when relevant. Some need fortified breast milk, a specialist formula or feeding support; the neonatal team should guide these decisions.

Lung or heart conditions can also make feeding harder and increase the energy needed for everyday activity. The effect varies with the condition and treatment, so a single claim that every baby with heart disease burns 40% more energy is not useful for planning feeds. A specialist can set individual energy, volume and follow-up goals, including any fluid limits.

Use growth charts as a pattern, not a pass-or-fail score

The care team considers weight alongside length, head growth and previous measurements. A percentile describes position relative to a reference group; it is not a grade. A baby can be naturally small and healthy, while a falling pattern or low weight relative to length may need assessment. Current AAP guidance also uses z-scores to help describe the degree of change.

WHO growth standards are recommended in the United States from birth to two years for both breastfed and formula-fed babies. The chart is not selected simply by choosing WHO for breast milk and CDC for formula. Feeding-related growth patterns and local guidance still matter, and preterm babies may need a different assessment. Ask the clinician to explain your baby’s own trajectory.

Swallowing and nappies add information, not certainty

During a feed, look and listen for swallowing rather than only counting minutes of sucking. For bottle feeds, note what was offered and what was taken without pressuring the baby to finish. After the early newborn transition, around six or more wet nappies a day is often reassuring, but nappy expectations vary with age.

Wet nappies do not prove that calorie intake or weight gain is adequate. Use them alongside stool changes, alertness, feeding and measured growth. A trained professional may use a before-and-after feed weight to estimate milk transfer during that feed. One such measurement does not describe every feed or the whole day, and ordinary household scales may not be precise enough.

Supporting milk supply without a promised herbal fix

Effective, regular milk removal can help milk production. A plan may include improving attachment, offering feeds more often or expressing when the baby cannot transfer enough. Skin-to-skin contact, practical help and rest can support the process, but there is no guarantee that simply feeding every one or two hours will resolve every cause of low supply.

Fenugreek, fennel, milk thistle and dates are sometimes promoted as milk boosters. Evidence is limited and uneven, and herbs can have side effects, variable contents and medicine interactions. Postnatal vitamins support particular nutritional needs; they are not a universal treatment for low milk supply. Discuss supplements with the team rather than delaying needed infant nutrition while trying them.

Increase usable intake with a clear feeding plan

Breast-milk fat content changes during and between feeds; there is not a rigid switch from one kind of milk to another. The goal is effective transfer and enough total intake, not keeping a tired baby at one breast until it is supposedly empty. A lactation professional can advise when to switch sides, use breast compressions or express.

If additional milk is needed, the plan may use expressed breast milk and, when appropriate, formula or another clinically suitable option. Support ongoing breastfeeding if that is your goal, but do not delay required supplementation. Ask how much to offer, how to give it, how to support supply and when to reassess rather than improvising an open-ended top-up routine.

Formula concentration and catch-up feeding need supervision

Prepare formula with exactly the water and powder amounts on the instructions unless a clinician has prescribed a specific alternative recipe. Adding extra powder can cause harm, while extra water reduces nutrition and can also be dangerous. Do not add sugar, cereal or other ingredients to make a bottle more fattening.

Some babies need higher-energy feeds or fortification under specialist guidance. The team should explain the recipe, hygiene, daily amount and signs of intolerance. Substantial undernutrition needs a carefully monitored recovery plan rather than suddenly forcing very large feeds. If cost, access to formula, equipment or exhaustion makes the plan difficult, tell the team so practical support can be arranged.

Follow-up should include growth, development and family support

Persistent undernutrition can affect growth and development, which is why timely help matters. It does not mean that a baby with one slow interval will inevitably have developmental problems. A paediatrician, dietitian and feeding specialist may work together, with the frequency of weight checks matched to the level of concern.

Agree a measurable plan and a date for review. Excessive home weighing can increase anxiety and make normal short-term variation look alarming. Seek help sooner if feeds worsen, wet nappies fall, the baby becomes hard to wake or other illness signs appear. Improvement depends on the cause; do not accept a promise that every baby will catch up within a few days.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Assess growth over time alongside feeding, hydration, length and the baby’s overall condition; greater than 10% early weight loss requires evaluation.

Use individualized feeding support and follow-up. Do not change formula concentration or rely on herbal milk boosters to treat faltering weight.

How BeMama can help

Bring recent weights, feeding notes and nappy patterns to the appointment, then record the agreed feeding plan and next review date.

When to seek help

A baby who is difficult to wake, unable to feed, struggling to breathe or vomiting green fluid needs urgent medical help. Do not wait for the next weight check.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A baby’s growth pattern and condition matter more than a comparison with other babies.
  • Slow gain can reflect intake, nutrient loss or absorption, increased needs, or a combination.
  • A feeding observation can reveal problems that feed duration and bottle markings miss.
  • Use a clinician-led plan for supplements, fortification and follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 7–8% newborn weight loss always normal?

No single percentage is reassuring on its own. Age, feeding, hydration and the pattern matter. More than 10% needs evaluation, and symptoms can require help even with a smaller loss.

Should I wait three weeks for birth weight to return?

Do not wait if feeding or hydration is concerning. Many babies regain birth weight within 7–14 days; the care team should assess a slow recovery and agree follow-up.

Do six wet nappies prove my baby is gaining enough?

No. After the first few days they can be a useful hydration clue, but they do not replace feeding assessment and measured growth.

Does a formula-fed baby need a different chart from a breastfed baby?

Not simply because of milk type. In the US, WHO standards are recommended for both from birth to two years; preterm assessment and local guidance may differ.

Is all spit-up a sign that calories are not being absorbed?

No. Small spit-ups are common in well-growing babies. Significant vomiting or feeding distress with poor growth needs assessment, and green or persistently forceful vomiting is urgent.

Should I cut out dairy and gluten myself?

Ask for assessment first. Unnecessary exclusions can reduce nutrition, and removing gluten before coeliac testing can affect the results.

Will fenugreek or milk thistle fix low supply?

They are not reliable substitutes for assessing milk transfer and supply. Evidence is limited and they can cause adverse effects or interactions.

Should I keep the baby on one breast until all the hindmilk is finished?

There is no fixed switch or completely empty breast to target. Effective transfer and enough total intake matter; get help with attachment, switching sides and supplementation if needed.

Can I add extra formula powder to increase calories?

Only follow a specific clinician-prescribed recipe. Otherwise use the exact product instructions; changing the concentration can harm your baby.

When is slow gain an urgent problem?

Seek urgent help if your baby is difficult to wake, cannot feed, struggles to breathe, has markedly fewer wet nappies or has concerning vomiting. Do not wait for a routine review.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
